scenario: AITA for not believing my coworker about “chronic pain”? | I have a coworker in his mid 30s who claims to suffer from chronic pain. Frankly, I think it’s a load of crap. Some days he’s limping around the office or even calls in sick claiming he’s in too bad of pain to come into the office. He’ll be wincing and just sitting in his chair. He claims it’s from a botched surgery. Somehow he’s been granted FMLA. There are plenty of other days though when he’s walking around just fine, even talking walks in the park across from our office or standing around at a coworker’s desk laughing while they talk. I’ve made comments like “Gee, you look like you’re really hurting!” on those days and he just says “I’m having a good day. They happen.” Recently he started using a cane as a prop, which is when I confronted him. There’s no way it’s legitimate need. I asked him just how bad his surgery was that now he needs a cane, adding that it was taking the act a bit too far. He pulled up his shirt and revealed a dinky little 4” scar near his waist. I said laughed and said “That’s why you’re stumbling around?” He replied “This is the outside. I hope you get to feel what I feel, asshole.” Then he shuffled away with his cane and next thing I know I’m getting talked to by our boss about how I’m treating Mr. Pain and that it’s inappropriate. When I told my boss I knew he was faking, he told me “his doctors know more than you” and that if I ever voiced doubt about the coworker in the office again, I’d be looking for a new job.

This type of group is often referred to as a "community of practice" or a "values-based community." Research suggests that being part of a community that shares your values and goals can have a positive influence on personal growth, well-being, and behavior. Here are a few ways in which a values-based community can push people to be better: 1. **Social support**: Being surrounded by people who care about you and share your values can provide a sense of security and motivation to strive for personal growth. 2. **Accountability**: When you're part of a community that expects certain standards of behavior, you're more likely to hold yourself to those standards and be accountable for your actions. 3. **Role modeling**: Observing and learning from others who embody the values you aspire to can inspire and motivate you to adopt similar behaviors and attitudes. 4. **Feedback and reflection**: Engaging in open and honest discussions with others who share your values can help you reflect on your actions, identify areas for improvement, and receive constructive feedback. 5. **Sense of purpose**: Being part of a community that shares your values can give you a sense of purpose and direction, which can motivate you to work towards common goals and strive for personal growth. While a values-based community may not provide the same level of structure or dogma as a religious community, it can still offer a sense of belonging, support, and guidance that can help individuals grow and develop as people. In your case, having a group of people you respect and share values with can be a powerful catalyst for personal growth. By engaging in open and honest discussions, sharing experiences, and learning from one another, you can create a supportive environment that encourages and motivates you to be your best self. What do you personally think about this — is it right or wrong, and why?
